**Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR)** and **BM25** differ mainly in how they represent and match text:

- **Representation:** BM25 represents queries and passages as high-dimensional sparse vectors and retrieves through weighted keyword matching with an inverted index. DPR learns dense embeddings for questions and passages using a dual-encoder framework.
- **Matching:** BM25 depends strongly on token overlap and selective keywords. DPR can retrieve semantically related passages even when queries and passages use different tokens, such as synonyms or paraphrases.
- **Strengths and weaknesses:** BM25 is effective when rare, salient phrases or exact terms matter. DPR better captures lexical variation and semantic relationships, but may fail to represent rare salient phrases adequately.
- **Retrieval quality:** In the cited experiments, DPR outperformed BM25 on four of five open-domain QA datasets, with a larger advantage at smaller retrieval depths—for example, **78.4% versus 59.1% top-20 accuracy** on Natural Questions. SQuAD was the exception.
- **Indexing and speed:** BM25 uses an inverted index, whereas DPR can use a vector index such as FAISS. One reported DPR setup processed 995 questions per second while returning 100 passages per question.

In short, **BM25 retrieves by lexical overlap; DPR retrieves by learned semantic similarity**.
per_question.reference: DPR learns dense low-dimensional embeddings of questions and passages with a dual-encoder (BERT-based) trained on question-passage pairs and retrieves by inner-product similarity, instead of relying on sparse term matching.
